prompt: Ana killed the shop's process with `kill -9`, and three seconds later it was serving again. What brought it back?
hint: Look at the last line of `compose.yaml`.

choices.text: Compose, which watches the containers it started
choices.why: Compose read the file once, at `up`, and was not running when the process died.

choices.text: The Docker daemon, applying `restart: always`
choices.why: Right. The policy is kept by the daemon on that machine, which saw the exit and started the container again.

choices.text: Nothing: `SIGKILL` cannot stop a container's process
choices.why: It did stop it; the restart count went from 0 to 1 because the process exited.

choices.text: The shop itself, which caught the signal and restarted
choices.why: No program can catch `SIGKILL`; that is the point of using it here.

prompt: `docker compose up -d --scale web=3` stopped with `Bind for 0.0.0.0:8080 failed: port is already allocated`. What is the underlying limit?
hint: Three containers, one machine, one published port.

choices.text: Compose can only run one replica of a service
choices.why: It created `shop-web-2` and `shop-web-3`; what failed was publishing their port.

choices.text: The image was built to listen on one port
choices.why: Each container has its own network namespace, so each can listen on 8080 inside it; the clash is on the laptop.

choices.text: The laptop ran out of memory for a third copy
choices.why: The error names a port, not memory.

choices.text: One port of one machine can belong to one process
choices.why: Right. The first copy owns 8080 on the host; the others need a proxy in front or ports of their own.

prompt: Ana adds a second laptop and runs the same `compose.yaml` on both, each with `restart: always`. The first laptop loses power. What happens to the copy that was running on it?
hint: Who keeps the restart policy, and where does it live?

choices.text: The second laptop's daemon starts it there
choices.why: Each daemon knows only its own containers; nothing tells the second one that a copy is missing.

choices.text: It is gone until the first laptop comes back
choices.why: Right. The policy lived in the first laptop's daemon and went down with it; the second laptop keeps its own copy and no more.

choices.text: Compose moves it, since both laptops share one file
choices.why: The file is the same, but nothing reads it continuously on either machine.

choices.text: Both copies stop, because the two daemons are linked
choices.why: Two plain Docker daemons are not linked at all; the second copy keeps running.

prompt: During the update from `shop:1.0` to `shop:1.1`, how many of the probe's 300 requests got no answer?
After the update, the shop answered `shop 1.1 on cdb0f6d432ff`, where it had said `7f1b64994482` before. What does the new hostname tell you?
hint: The hostname is the start of the container's id.

choices.text: The same container was renamed after its image changed
choices.why: A container's id is fixed for its life; a new id is a new container.

choices.text: Compose moved the container to a different network
choices.why: The network `shop_default` stayed; what changed was the container.

choices.text: The old container was removed and a new one created
choices.why: Right. A container is replaced, never updated in place, and the gap is the time between the two.

choices.text: The probe reached a second replica started for the update
choices.why: There was only ever one replica; that is why requests were refused.

prompt: Which of these does an update without a gap need, that the one-machine setup did not have? Choose all that apply.
hint: Think of the order: start, wait, move, stop.

choices.text: Two copies running at the same moment
choices.why: Right: the new one has to be up before the old one goes.

choices.text: Something in front that decides which copy gets a request
choices.why: Right: moving the traffic needs a place where traffic is routed.

choices.text: A faster disk, so the new container starts sooner
choices.why: A faster start shortens the gap without closing it; the order is still stop, then start.

choices.text: A signal that the new copy is ready, not just started
choices.why: Right: otherwise traffic moves to a process that is still loading.

choices.text: A new image tag for every version
choices.why: The update already used `shop:1.1`; tags name versions, they do not order the swap.

prompt: What does an orchestrator do that `docker compose up` does not?
hint: Both read a description of what should run. The difference is when.

choices.text: It reads a file that describes the containers
choices.why: So does Compose; `compose.yaml` is such a file.

choices.text: It starts containers from images
choices.why: Compose does that too, through the Docker daemon.

choices.text: It keeps comparing that description with what is running, and acts on the difference
choices.why: Right. Compose reads the file when somebody types `up` and stops looking; the loop never stops.

choices.text: It restarts a process that crashes
choices.why: The Docker daemon already did that in the first section, with `restart: always`.

prompt: Match each need with what handles it on a cluster.
hint: The table in this section names a lesson for each.

pairs.right: A Service in front of them
Start, wait for ready, then stop
A controller that changes the count
Its copies started on the machines left

right_distractors: A restart policy on each machine's daemon

prompt: A team runs one internal tool on one virtual machine, updates it once a month after hours, and nobody uses it at night. Which reading of this lesson fits them best?
hint: Weigh the twelve requests against the price paid before the first one.

choices.text: Kubernetes, since a gap during updates is never acceptable
choices.why: Nobody is using it during the gap; the twelve requests would hit no one.

choices.text: Compose is enough; the gaps fall where nobody is asking
choices.why: Right. The orchestrator's price is paid up front, and here it would buy almost nothing.

choices.text: Neither: a tool on one machine should not run in a container
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson argues against containers on one machine; Compose is shown working well there.

choices.text: Kubernetes, because its restart policy is the stronger one
choices.why: On one machine the Docker daemon already restarts a crashed process; that is not what a cluster is for.

prompt: Put the steps of an update without a gap in order.
hint: The old copy is the last thing to go.
items: Start a copy of the new version
Wait until the new copy answers as ready
Send the traffic to the new copy
trap: Stopping the old copy any earlier is the Compose order, and the gap it measured.
